headline: Midjourney's Artist List Leak Spawns a Retaliatory Style Tool
lede: When a leaked database of more than 16,000 artists allegedly used without consent to train Midjourney's image generator went viral in January 2024, it crystallised a grievance that had been building since generative AI emerged: creative work harvested at scale, without payment or permission. A rival platform, Higgsfield AI, is now marketing a feature called *Steal* as poetic payback — a tool to replicate Midjourney's own visual output.
body:
The spreadsheet that ignited the controversy, labelled "Midjourney Style List," was retrieved from Midjourney's development environment and shared publicly before access was restricted. It listed the names of painters, cartoonists, sculptors, and illustrators — among them Frida Kahlo, Walt Disney, and Yayoi Kusama — whose styles had apparently been preloaded as reference material. Screenshots shared by artist Jon Lam showed Midjourney developers discussing sourcing artist names from Wikipedia to enrich the model's ability to mimic specific styles on command.

Many names from the spreadsheet also appeared in court documents filed in a 2023 **class-action lawsuit** against Midjourney. That suit argues the company systematically ingested copyrighted artwork to train its model without compensating or notifying creators. The legal territory remains uncertain: in the United States, courts have not yet settled whether training a model on copyrighted images constitutes infringement, fair use, or something in between.

Into this charged atmosphere, Higgsfield AI has introduced a feature it markets under the name *Steal* — framed by the poster as a tool for artists to extract or reproduce Midjourney's stylistic output. The framing is deliberately provocative: if Midjourney can harvest artistic styles, why shouldn't users harvest Midjourney's?

The irony cuts both ways. A tool designed to mimic one AI platform's visual character is, structurally, doing the same thing critics accuse Midjourney of doing to human artists. Whether it constitutes a meaningful act of redress for the 16,000-plus artists on the leaked list — or merely transfers the appropriation one layer up — is a question the tweet does not pause to ask.

concepts.definition: The images, text, or other content an AI model learns from during development. In image generation, the model studies millions of examples to learn how to produce visual output. The question of whether using copyrighted work as training data infringes copyright is actively contested in courts.

An AI's ability to generate images that closely resemble the distinctive look of a specific artist or platform. Style itself is generally not copyrightable under US law, but the training images used to teach that mimicry may be — a tension at the heart of the ongoing lawsuits.

A legal action in which a large group of plaintiffs with similar claims sue a defendant collectively. In 2023, a group of artists filed such a suit against Midjourney and other AI image companies, alleging their work was used without consent to train commercial AI products.

fact_check: The tweet frames using Higgsfield Steal as artists "taking back" from Midjourney, but this overstates what the tool does. Mimicking Midjourney's output style does not compensate the original artists whose work allegedly trained that model, nor does it advance the litigation. The characterisation of Midjourney's actions as definitively "stealing" also runs ahead of the law: as of early 2024, no court had issued a final ruling that training on copyrighted images constitutes infringement. The lawsuit was ongoing.
thread_summary: This is post 1 of 6 in a thread by @techhalla. The remaining posts (2–6) are not included in the bookmark, but based on the framing they likely walk through specific examples of using Higgsfield Steal to reproduce Midjourney-style imagery.
